title: Free-rider problem

definition.text: A market failure that happens when people who benefit from a shared resource or public good pay nothing, or too little, for it.

facts.text: A coastal town's lighthouse helps ships from many countries, even though those ships pay nothing toward its costs.
Because no one can be kept from using a public good, each person has little reason to help pay for it.
Free riding leads to too little of a good being produced or too much being used up, which is wasteful for society.
When asked how much money they would pay for a public good, people tend to understate how much they value it.
Even though people tend to cooperate by nature, the presence of free riders has been shown to make cooperation break down.
Climate change is often framed as a free-rider problem: every country gains from others cutting emissions, but each would lose by switching to a low-carbon economy itself.
Shown as a prisoner's dilemma, if two people should share the cost of a fire station and both refuse to pay, society gets nothing.
Low-cost pooling of contributions, as in internet crowdfunding where no money changes hands until a goal is met, is one way around the problem.

title: Assurance contract

definition.text: An agreement in which people pledge money toward a public good only if enough others also pledge; otherwise the good is not built and the money is returned.

facts.text: In a dominant assurance contract, an entrepreneur refunds pledges plus an extra sum if the target is missed, and earns a fee if it is met.
This makes pledging the best move for each person whatever others do, which game theory calls a dominant strategy.
First proposed by Bagnoli and Lipman in 1989, they work best in small groups of easily identified people, and crowdfunding sites such as Kickstarter use them.

title: Intellectual property as an exclusion mechanism
article: Free-rider problem#Introducing an exclusion mechanism (club goods)

definition.text: Using laws such as copyright and patents to stop people copying an information good, turning a public good into a club good.

facts.text: These laws can solve free riding, but they give owners monopoly power, so the result is not fully efficient.
In the United States, patent rights encourage drug companies to charge prices above the cost of making one more dose.

title: Social sanctions against free riders
article: Free-rider problem#Non-altruistic social sanctions (common property regimes)

definition.text: Punishments that group members impose on those who use a shared resource without contributing, as a way to keep cooperation going without the state.

facts.text: Punishing costs the punisher, so groups often reward members who sanction free riders.
Paying for enforcement is not perfectly efficient, but it is often cheaper than letting the resource run down.
People sometimes punish free riders even without any reward, though whether such costly punishment explains cooperation is disputed.

related: Ostrom's design principles for the commons
contested_note: Researchers dispute whether costly punishment of free riders can explain cooperation.

title: Property rights

definition.text: The rules that decide who owns a resource or good and how it may be used.

facts.text: Resources can be owned by individuals, associations, collectives or governments.
Property rights have three parts: the right to use a good, the right to earn income from it, and the right to sell, change, abandon or destroy it.
Well-enforced property rights give people reasons to invest, innovate and trade, which makes markets work better.
Governments can create property rights through direct rules such as discharge limits, or through market tools such as taxes and tradable permits.
An emissions trading scheme works by setting up property rights for the atmosphere.
Secure rights make resources harder to exploit, so people are less likely to use them unsustainably.
Studying former European colonies, Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson found strong evidence that institutions giving secure property rights lead to prosperity.

distinct_from: Property rights theory of the firm

title: Types of property regimes

definition.text: The main ways a resource can be held, open access, public, private or common property, sorted by whether others can be kept out and whether use leaves less for others.

facts.text: Open-access property is owned by nobody, nobody manages it and access is not controlled; an unregulated forest is an example.
Open access can exist because ownership was never set up in law, or because keeping people out costs more than it is worth.
Public or state property is owned by the public, with access and use controlled by a government agency.
Private property is controlled by its owner or owners; a cellphone is an example because only one person can use it and it must be bought.
Common or collective property in the legal sense is owned by a group whose members jointly control access, use and exclusion.

title: Property rights theory of the firm

definition.text: The theory, built by Grossman, Hart and Moore, that because contracts can never cover every future event, ownership matters by deciding who controls decisions when no agreement is reached.

facts.text: Since deals will be renegotiated, each party expects only part of the return on its investment and so invests too little, the hold-up problem.
The approach explains the pros and cons of merging firms and has also been applied to public good provision and privatization.

title: Lockean labor theory of property

definition.text: John Locke's idea that a person who mixes their labor with an unowned resource comes to own the result, as long as enough of as good quality is left for others.

facts.text: Locke set out the theory in his Second Treatise of Government (1689), starting from the claim that each person owns their own self.
The condition that 'enough and as good' must remain for others is called the Lockean proviso.
Libertarians cite the tragedy of the commons as what happens when governments forbid people to claim resources in the Lockean way.

distinct_from: Property rights theory of the firm

definition.text: A good is rival when one person's use of it stops or reduces others' use of it at the same time.

facts.text: An apple is rival: once one person eats it, no one else can.
A good is non-rival when serving one more person costs nothing extra; a TV broadcast, a scenic view, clean air and street lights are examples.
Non-rivalry does not mean a good is cheap to provide in total, only that the cost of one more user is zero.
Roads, the internet and courts are non-rival only up to a point, after which congestion slows everyone, so economists now treat rivalry as a scale rather than a yes-or-no.
Paul Samuelson introduced non-rival consumption in 1954 to tell private from public goods, and Richard Musgrave later added rivalry and excludability as criteria.

definition.text: A good that becomes more valuable to each user the more other people use it.

facts.text: Steven Weber introduced the idea in 2004, noting that free and open-source software gets better for everyone as more people use it.
Any natural language is anti-rival, because it is more useful the more people speak it.
Efforts against climate change are perversely anti-rival: a free-riding country still gains from others' efforts.
